_about: An English crib of the Instituta Cnuti, relatively literal, made with Claude (Anthropic) in November 2026 for this edition. Keyed as data/incn-reading.json (clause id | In Cn chapter; rubrics by clause id). Liebermann’s kinds of type are carried over onto the English words that render the marked Latin: hi rend bold / spaced / small, seg type recension, seg type parallel. tools/incn/reading.py adds it to the reading view.

<seg type="parallel"><label>H Di</label>Here begin <hi rend="spaced">certain</hi> institutes concerning the laws of the kings of the English (<hi rend="italic">H</hi>; <hi rend="spaced">institutes according to King Cnut</hi> of the English <hi rend="italic">Di</hi>).</seg><seg type="parallel"><label>Ip Hunt (Interpolator of Henry of Huntingdon)</label>Here begins <hi rend="spaced">the law which in English is called <hi rend="italic">Danelage</hi>, but in Latin is rendered as the law of the Danes,</hi> instituted and diligently kept <hi rend="spaced">by the most invincible and glorious</hi> <hi rend="small">king of the English, Danes, Norwegians, Swedes</hi>, Cnut.</seg>
crib.ICn_Prol|I Prol–I 5.2d: This is the institution which King Cnut, with the <hi rend="spaced">counsel of the chief men</hi>, his wise men, instituted to the praise of God and the honour of himself and the benefit <hi rend="bold">of the whole kingdom over which he ruled</hi>.
crib.ICn_1|I Prol–I 5.2d: First, that above all things he would always worship one God, love, honour [him], keep with one mind the one faith of Christ, guard the churches of God in peace and security, <hi rend="spaced">and the same</hi> frequent more often, <hi rend="bold">for the quiet and stability of his kingdom and for …</hi>
crib.ICn_2|I Prol–I 5.2d: … <hi rend="spaced">the salvation of his body and soul</hi>.
crib.ICn_2-1|I Prol–I 5.2d: Every church <hi rend="spaced">therefore</hi> according to the rule of justice <hi rend="spaced">ought</hi> to be in God's own peace and security; and it befits every Christian <hi rend="spaced">to show the churches of God</hi> the greatest reverence; for the peace and security of God is to be earned and held with the utmost diligence, and next the peace and security of the king.
crib.ICn_2-2|I Prol–I 5.2d: Wherefore it is most just that the peace of the churches of God within the walls and the peace <hi rend="spaced">given by the hand</hi> of a Christian king always stand inviolate; and whoever breaks either, <hi rend="spaced">namely the peace of the church or of the king</hi>, let him lose <hi rend="spaced">all his goods</hi> and life, unless the king will spare him.
crib.ICn_2-3|I Prol–I 5.2d: But if henceforth anyone so violates the peace of the churches of God that he <hi rend="spaced">commits homicide</hi> within the walls, this shall be unatonable, and let everyone who <hi rend="spaced">wishes</hi> to be a friend of God pursue such a man, unless it happens that he escapes and seeks such a place <hi rend="bold">or man</hi> that for this <hi rend="spaced">seeking</hi> the king grants him his life, <hi rend="spaced">yet</hi> on condition of full amends.
crib.ICn_2-5|I Prol–I 5.2d: But if he comes to amends, and the king permits it, before all things let him fully make amends for the broken peace of the church according to the full forfeiture, <hi rend="spaced">which the English name</hi> <hi rend="italic">múndbrece</hi> [breach of protection], <seg type="recension">(and)</seg> obtain reconciliation for the church, <seg type="recension">(and)</seg> pay <hi rend="spaced">full amends</hi> to the kinsmen and the lord of the slain man, which the English <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">mæibote</hi> and <hi rend="italic">manbote</hi> [compensation to kin and to lord], and above all make satisfaction to God <hi rend="bold">according to the bishop's decree</hi>.
crib.ICn_3|I Prol–I 5.2d: If <hi rend="spaced">however</hi> the peace of the church is otherwise violated by the living, either by fighting or by <hi rend="spaced">robbing</hi> or by whatever it may be,
crib.ICn_3a|I Prol–I 5.2d: first of all let amends always be made to the church according to its quality <seg type="recension">(and dignity)</seg>.
crib.ICn_3-1|I Prol–I 5.2d: <hi rend="spaced">For</hi> not all churches are of <hi rend="spaced">one and the same</hi> honour, although they have <hi rend="spaced">one and the same</hi> consecration.
crib.ICn_3-2|I Prol–I 5.2d: The chief churches <hi rend="spaced">however</hi>, <hi rend="bold">such as bishoprics </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="bold">(and abbeys)</hi></seg><hi rend="bold">,</hi> <hi rend="spaced">ought to have</hi> such <hi rend="spaced">amends</hi> for violated peace according to the law of the English: the king's <hi rend="italic">mund</hi> [protection], that is five pounds; <hi rend="bold">but according to the law of the Danes, certainly, eight pounds.</hi><seg type="parallel"><label>Cb</label>But middling churches, <hi rend="bold">such as abbeys and houses of canons,</hi> according to the king's forfeiture, namely <hi rend="bold">XXC</hi> shillings, <hi rend="bold">that is four pounds.</hi> The lesser churches, that is where service is held and yet they have a cemetery, 60 shillings, <hi rend="bold">that is three pounds.</hi> <hi rend="spaced">But the least churches</hi>, which <hi rend="spaced">the English</hi> call <hi rend="italic">feldcherche</hi> [field-church], that is those lacking a cemetery, 30 shillings.</seg><seg type="parallel"><label>H Di Lb S Ct Jo</label>But for a middling church <hi rend="bold">two pounds,</hi> that is according to the king's forfeiture, and further for a lesser church, that is where little service is held and yet it has a cemetery, the forfeiture is <hi rend="bold">one pound;</hi> but for the least church, which the English call <hi rend="italic">feldcirice</hi> [field-church], <hi rend="bold">eighty pence.</hi></seg>
crib.ICn_4|I Prol–I 5.2d: <hi rend="spaced">Therefore</hi> it most justly befits all Christians always to venerate <seg type="recension">(with)</seg> the utmost diligence <hi rend="spaced">the relics of the saints</hi>, and to honour the ordained and hallowed houses and each order according to its measure <hi rend="bold">and its life</hi>.
crib.ICn_4-1|I Prol–I 5.2d: Therefore let him who <hi rend="bold">wishes</hi> know that much and great is what the priest has to do for the people for their need <seg type="recension">(benefit)</seg>, if he himself rightly pleases the Lord <seg type="recension">(who <hi rend="spaced">desires and strives</hi> to please <hi rend="spaced">his</hi> Lord justly)</seg>.
crib.ICn_4-2|I Prol–I 5.2d: For great is the adjuration and greater the consecration, which cast out demons and put them to flight, whenever <hi rend="spaced">an infant is baptized</hi> or the Lord's body is consecrated; <hi rend="spaced">certainly</hi> angels fly around and by God's power give help to the priest and protect his deeds, whenever they serve Christ worthily.
crib.ICn_4-3|I Prol–I 5.2d: So too they always do, when they devoutly invoke Christ for the people's need and pour out prayers to <hi rend="spaced">God</hi>; and therefore in such an order <seg type="recension">(as <hi rend="spaced">we have said</hi>)</seg> there ought to be great discretion and <hi rend="spaced">consideration</hi>.
crib.ICn_5|I Prol–I 5.2d: If it happens that a priest living by rule and <hi rend="spaced">chastely</hi> is accused of theft or of sorcery or of any such <seg type="recension">(similar)</seg> matter, and he denies it, he shall clear himself thus, if he dares: let him celebrate mass and clear himself alone by the body of the Lord of a single accusation, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">anfealde spæce</hi> [single charge].
crib.ICn_5-1|I Prol–I 5.2d: If <hi rend="spaced">however</hi> a deacon who lives by rule is accused by a single accusation, let him clear himself, taking two deacons with him.
crib.ICn_5-1a|I Prol–I 5.2d: And if there are three accusations, let him take six <hi rend="spaced">with him</hi> and himself be the seventh <seg type="recension">(having taken six <hi rend="spaced">deacons</hi> with him, let him so clear himself)</seg>.
crib.ICn_5-2|I Prol–I 5.2d: If a common <seg type="recension">(popular)</seg> priest, who does not live by rule, is accused by a <hi rend="spaced">single</hi> accusation <seg type="recension">(of the above-said)</seg>, let him clear himself like a deacon who lives by rule.
crib.ICn_5-2a|I Prol–I 5.2d: If an ordained <hi rend="bold">stranger or</hi> <hi rend="bold">foreigner</hi> is accused of the <hi rend="spaced">already named</hi> crimes, who has no helper <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">other aid</hi>)</seg>, let him go to the blessed bread, which <hi rend="spaced">the English</hi> <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">corsnade</hi> [<hi rend="italic">corsnæd</hi>, ordeal morsel], and there he will find what pleases God.
crib.ICn_5-2b|I Prol–I 5.2d: If any ordained man is accused of homicide, that he had been in it by deed or by counsel, let him clear himself with his kinsmen, who can pay the amends or bear [the feud].
crib.ICn_5-2c|I Prol–I 5.2d: If he has no kinsmen, let him clear himself with companions or begin to fast and so go to the blessed bread, <hi rend="spaced">of which we spoke above</hi>, and there he will find what has pleased God <seg type="recension">(let him find what pleases God)</seg>.
crib.ICn_5-2d|I Prol–I 5.2d: No monk of a monastery ought to pay amends for homicide nor seek amends for homicide, <hi rend="bold">though he be a kinsman of the slayer</hi> <seg type="recension"><hi rend="bold">(of the slayers)</hi></seg><hi rend="bold"> or of the slain</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">because</hi> when he enters the <hi rend="spaced">monastery</hi> to keep the rule, he leaves behind <hi rend="spaced">the things that are secular</hi> . . . .
crib.Af_20|I 5.2e: If anyone commends money <hi rend="bold">or any such thing</hi> to another man's monk <hi rend="spaced">for safekeeping</hi> without the leave of his <hi rend="bold">prelate</hi>, and <hi rend="spaced">the monk loses it, let it be lost to him who</hi> without the leave of <hi rend="spaced">his</hi> <hi rend="bold">prelate</hi> <hi rend="spaced">commended it to the monk</hi> . . . .
crib.ICn_5a|I 5.3–9: And if there are three <hi rend="spaced">accusations</hi>, let him clear himself, taking two priests with him, <hi rend="spaced">as</hi> we said before, if he dares . . . .
crib.ICn_5-3|I 5.3–9: A priest, if he <hi rend="bold">has been accused and convicted</hi> that he stood in false witness or swore with perjurers or was an accomplice or privy to theft, let him be put out of the communion and fellowship of the ordained and lose their noble rank, <hi rend="bold">which the English call <hi rend="italic">þegenscipe</hi></hi> [thegnship], unless he makes deeper satisfaction to God and men according to his bishop's command, and finds sureties that from that time on he will cease from such <hi rend="spaced">works</hi>.
crib.ICn_5-4|I 5.3–9: But if he <hi rend="spaced">denies</hi> it and wishes to clear himself, let him clear himself according to the manner and quantity of the guilt.
crib.ICn_6|I 5.3–9: This also we decree, that <hi rend="spaced">everyone</hi>, of whatever order <hi rend="spaced">or sex he be</hi>, keep his order.
crib.ICn_6a|I 5.3–9: And especially we command this to the servants and handmaids of God, namely bishops, abbots, <hi rend="spaced">abbesses</hi>, monks, holy women, canons, <hi rend="spaced">priests</hi>, nuns, that they live by rule <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">as we have said</hi>)</seg> according to the order of each,
crib.ICn_6-1|I 5.3–9: keep chastity, beware of the wrath of God <hi rend="bold">and chasten others by living and admonishing,</hi> so that they guard themselves from the fire of hell.
crib.ICn_6-2|I 5.3–9: For the <hi rend="spaced">bishops</hi> and the other orders whom I <hi rend="spaced">have mentioned above</hi> <seg type="recension">(named)</seg> know very well that it is in no way lawful for them to have intercourse with women nor to lie with them.
crib.ICn_6-2a|I 5.3–9: But he who henceforth wishes <seg type="recension">(strives)</seg> to cease from such <hi rend="spaced">work</hi> and to keep chastity, let him have the mercy of God and, according to worldly dignity, the noble rank <hi rend="spaced">which</hi> <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">þegenscipe</hi> [thegnship].
crib.ICn_6-3|I 5.3–9: We also earnestly <hi rend="spaced">pray</hi> every Christian to avoid fornication and to keep diligently the laws and <hi rend="spaced">precepts</hi> of God.
crib.ICn_7|I 5.3–9: This also we ask and command in the name of the <hi rend="spaced">Lord</hi>, that no Christian take to himself a wife within the sixth <hi rend="bold">knee</hi> [degree], nor the widow who <hi rend="spaced">was</hi> thus <hi rend="spaced">joined</hi> to a near kinsman, nor a kinswoman of the wife whom he had before;
crib.ICn_7-1|I 5.3–9: nor his fellow godparent, nor a consecrated <hi rend="bold">holy woman</hi> or nun, nor another man's widow, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">oþres <hi rend="bold">mannes</hi> ælǽte</hi> [another man's relict]: to such, <hi rend="spaced">as we said</hi>, let no Christian join himself;
crib.ICn_7-3|I 5.3–9: nor let him have more than one wife, who is lawfully betrothed to him, and with her alone, while she lives, <hi rend="bold">healthy and sick,</hi> let him be content.
crib.ICn_8|I 5.3–9: Let us <hi rend="spaced">also</hi> carefully strive to pay God's dues:
crib.ICn_8-1|I 5.3–9: namely the plough-alms, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">súlhælmesse</hi> [plough-alms], fifteen days after Easter, and <hi rend="spaced">the tithes of cattle and small beasts</hi> at Pentecost, [and] of the crops <seg type="recension">(and fruits)</seg> of the earth at the feast of All Saints.
crib.ICn_8-2|I 5.3–9: If anyone will not give the tithe, as the plough <hi rend="spaced">ploughs it</hi>, let the king's reeve and the bishop's reeve, and also the reeve of the lord whose land it is <hi rend="bold">in chief</hi>, and the priest of the church to <hi rend="spaced">which</hi> that tithe belongs <hi rend="spaced">go to</hi> him <seg type="recension">(go)</seg>, and, <hi rend="bold">if they cannot otherwise,</hi> let them by force take <hi rend="spaced">away the tithe and give it</hi> to the church to which it <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">rightfully</hi>)</seg> belongs; but let them leave the ninth part to him <seg type="recension">(give to him)</seg> <hi rend="spaced">who unjustly</hi> <hi rend="spaced">retained the tithe</hi>; and let the eight parts be divided between the lord of the land and the bishop, whosesoever man he be, the king's, an <hi rend="bold">earl's</hi> or a free man of rank's (thegn's), whom the English call <hi rend="italic">þegen</hi> [thegn].
crib.ICn_9|I 5.3–9: The money <hi rend="spaced">however</hi> of <seg type="recension">(Saint)</seg> Peter, which the English call <hi rend="italic">Romescot</hi> [Rome-scot], <hi rend="spaced">is to be paid</hi> on the feast of Saint Peter <hi rend="bold">at the beginning of the month of August</hi> . . .
crib.IIEg_4-1|I 9a; b; c: And whoever has not paid on that day, <hi rend="bold">even if it is one</hi> <hi rend="bold">penny,</hi> <hi rend="spaced">who ought to give it</hi> <hi rend="spaced">and did not give it</hi>, let him take the same and thirty pence besides and carry it to Rome; <hi rend="spaced">and when he returns</hi>, let him bring back with him such a token that it be certain <hi rend="spaced">that he was at Rome</hi> <hi rend="spaced">and to Blessed Peter there thirty-one pence, as is decreed,</hi> has paid; and when he has come back home, let him pay the king <hi rend="bold">forty</hi> shillings.
crib.IIEg_4-2|I 9a; b; c: But if the same man withholds it a second time, <hi rend="spaced">let him do entirely the same</hi>.
crib.IIEg_4-3|I 9a; b; c: But if a third time he <hi rend="spaced">withholds it, let there be taken from</hi> him all his goods.
crib.ICn_12|I 12: . . . . <hi rend="spaced">The scot for lights,</hi> which the English <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">lihtgescot</hi> [light-scot], is to be given three times in the year <seg type="recension">(one)</seg> from each hide <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="bold">that is, <hi rend="italic">suling</hi></hi>)</seg>: wax worth one halfpenny on Easter Eve, on the eve of Saint Mary <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="bold">in the month of August</hi>)</seg>, <hi rend="spaced">on the eve of All</hi> Saints . . . .
crib.ICn_11|I 12a; b: If a free man of rank (thegn), whom <hi rend="spaced">the English</hi> call <hi rend="italic">þegen</hi> [thegn], has on his freehold <seg type="recension">(that is <hi rend="italic">bocland</hi> [bookland])</seg> a church which has a cemetery, let him give a third part of the tithe of his own <hi rend="spaced">land</hi> to that church.
crib.ICn_11-1|I 12a; b: But if <hi rend="spaced">another</hi> has a church which has no cemetery, let him give to his church out of <hi rend="spaced">the nine parts of his goods</hi> . . . .
crib.IIEg_1-1|I 12c: But let all tithes be rendered to the <hi rend="bold">old</hi> churches to which the parishioners <hi rend="bold">rightfully</hi> <hi rend="spaced">belong</hi>, both from the demesne of a noble, that is <hi rend="italic">þegnes</hi> [a thegn's], and from the land of villeins, <hi rend="spaced">that is</hi> <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">tunmannes</hi></hi> [townsmen's], as the plough ploughs it.
crib.ICn_10|I 12d: . . . . <hi rend="spaced">But every</hi> church gift, which <hi rend="spaced">the English</hi> call <hi rend="italic">ciricsceat</hi> [church-scot], is to be given to the old churches; and let it be paid on the feast of Saint Martin; if anyone withholds it beyond that day, let him render it to the bishop and pay it elevenfold and to the king <hi rend="bold">forty</hi> shillings . . .
crib.ICn_13|I 13–17.3: If anyone wishes <hi rend="spaced">to carry</hi> the <hi rend="spaced">body of his kinsman or</hi> <hi rend="spaced">friend</hi> from his own parish <hi rend="spaced">elsewhere</hi> for burial, let him first do right to the parish to which he belongs, namely the due which the English call <hi rend="italic">saulescot</hi> [soul-scot], which ought rightly <seg type="recension">(justly)</seg> to be paid at the open grave.
crib.ICn_14|I 13–17.3: Let the solemnities <hi rend="spaced">of the saints</hi> be diligently <seg type="recension">(by all)</seg> celebrated. And let Sundays be kept as holidays from the ninth hour of the <hi rend="spaced">preceding</hi> Saturday until the dawn of the <hi rend="spaced">following</hi> Monday; and let the other festivals and fasts be strictly kept, as <seg type="recension">(is <hi rend="spaced">decreed</hi> and commanded in the <hi rend="spaced">house</hi>)</seg> is commanded.
crib.ICn_15|I 13–17.3: We <hi rend="spaced">also</hi> forbid Sunday markets and all popular courts, unless there be very great necessity.
crib.ICn_15-1|I 13–17.3: <hi rend="spaced">Also the works</hi> of hunting and all secular business <hi rend="spaced">we prohibit</hi>.
crib.ICn_16|I 13–17.3: Also let the lawful fasts and the <hi rend="bold">vigils of the saints,</hi> namely of Saint Mary and of all the apostles, except Philip and James because of the Easter feasts, and the fasts of all Fridays, unless it be a festival, <hi rend="spaced">be kept</hi>.
crib.ICn_16-1|I 13–17.3: From Easter until Pentecost however let no one fast, unless it be enjoined <hi rend="bold">for public</hi> penance; and from the day of the Lord's nativity until the octave of Epiphany <hi rend="spaced">let the same be observed</hi>.
crib.ICn_17|I 13–17.3: On all feasts and fast days and the days of Lent, and from the Lord's Advent until eight days after the <hi rend="bold">octave</hi> of Epiphany, and from Septuagesima until fifteen days after Easter, we forbid <hi rend="spaced">all</hi> ordeals <hi rend="bold">of iron and water</hi> and <hi rend="spaced">every</hi> oath <hi rend="spaced">on God's part</hi>.
crib.ICn_17-1|I 13–17.3: [17, 1] The wise men <hi rend="spaced">of my kingdom with me</hi> have decreed that the feast of Saint Eadƿard the <hi rend="bold">king</hi> be celebrated on the 15th day before the Kalends of April and that of Saint Dunstan on the 14th day before the Kalends of June.
crib.ICn_17-2|I 13–17.3: [17, 2] On these days let there be peace and security for all Christians, and let strife <hi rend="spaced">and contention</hi> be put down.
crib.ICn_17-3|I 13–17.3: [17, 3] And if anyone <hi rend="spaced">owes another money or anything else</hi>, let him pay either before or after, <hi rend="spaced">at the nearest time</hi>.
crib.ICn_19|I 19: [19] Let us <hi rend="spaced">also</hi> do <hi rend="spaced">as</hi> is expedient <hi rend="spaced">for us</hi>: let us prepare <hi rend="spaced">ourselves and show ourselves such</hi> that at least three times in the year we <hi rend="spaced">may be able</hi> to receive communion of the Lord's body and blood.
crib.ICn_22|I 22–22.6: [22] <hi rend="spaced">Also</hi> every Christian <hi rend="spaced">ought</hi> to learn the ‘Pater noster’ and the ‘Credo in <hi rend="spaced">Deum</hi>’,
crib.ICn_22-1|I 22–22.6: [22, 1] because through the ‘<hi rend="spaced">Pater noster</hi>’ he ought to pray to <hi rend="spaced">God</hi> and through the ‘<hi rend="spaced">Credo</hi> <seg type="recension">(in Deum)</seg>’ show his faith.
crib.ICn_22-2|I 22–22.6: [22, 2] Christ himself first sang the ‘Pater noster’ and afterwards taught it to his disciples.
crib.ICn_22-3|I 22–22.6: [22, 3] For through the ‘<hi rend="spaced">Pater noster</hi>’ everyone can earn all that is needful in this world and in the next.
crib.ICn_22-4|I 22–22.6: [22, 4] But how can anyone pray to God with inmost heart unless he has right belief?
crib.ICn_22-5|I 22–22.6: [22, 5 <hi rend="italic">f</hi>.] <hi rend="spaced">It is fitting therefore</hi> that after the ‘Our Father’ he learn the ‘<hi rend="spaced">I believe in God</hi>’, <hi rend="spaced">so that he may show that he has the faith of Christ</hi>. And truly I say to you: he is not a perfect Christian <hi rend="spaced">nor is he worthy</hi> to receive the body and blood of the Lord, nor to lift anyone from baptism, nor for <hi rend="spaced">confirmation</hi> before the bishop to hold any<hi rend="spaced">one, and truly he is not worthy that his body be buried among the bodies of Christians</hi>, who does not know these <hi rend="spaced">two</hi>.
crib.IICn_Prol|II Prol–II 4a: This is also the secular ordinance which I, through the counsel <seg type="recension">(and <hi rend="spaced">consent</hi>)</seg> of my magnates, <hi rend="spaced">have resolved</hi> to keep throughout all <hi rend="spaced">my</hi> kingdom.
crib.IICn_1|II Prol–II 4a: First, that just laws be raised up, and unjust ones be put down and cast away;
crib.IICn_1-1|II Prol–II 4a: that laws <hi rend="spaced">be held</hi> rightly for rich and poor.
crib.IICn_2|II Prol–II 4a: But if <hi rend="bold">justice be burdensome,</hi> let him to whom the justice will then pertain consider the measure, as he wishes <hi rend="spaced">to be provided for by God</hi>, to whom <hi rend="spaced">we daily say</hi>: ‘And forgive us our debts, as we also <hi rend="spaced">forgive our debtors</hi>!’
crib.IICn_2-1|II Prol–II 4a: We also forbid that for a small matter Christians be delivered to death, <hi rend="bold">namely for theft or for such things,</hi> but in another way let them <hi rend="spaced">be corrected, for the sake of</hi> <hi rend="spaced">others</hi>, <hi rend="bold">lest the offences remain unpunished.</hi>
crib.IICn_3|II Prol–II 4a: And we <hi rend="spaced">forbid</hi> that Christians be sold to <hi rend="spaced">heathens</hi> outside <hi rend="spaced">this</hi> land or into heathendom, lest a <hi rend="spaced">Christian</hi> soul, which Christ himself redeemed with his <hi rend="spaced">blood</hi>, perish.
crib.IICn_4a|II Prol–II 4a: Sorcerers and <hi rend="spaced">sorceresses</hi> and evil-doers or <hi rend="spaced">open</hi> whores either <hi rend="spaced">be expelled</hi> from <hi rend="spaced">our</hi> kingdom or <hi rend="spaced">perish miserably</hi> in the land, or make amends <hi rend="spaced">to God and men publicly</hi>.
crib.IICn_5|II 5–9: We also forbid all superstition of the heathens,
crib.IICn_5-1|II 5–9: namely to worship idols, sun, moon, fire, water, springs, stones, to adore a <hi rend="spaced">leafy</hi> <hi rend="spaced">tree</hi>, a green <hi rend="bold">or dry</hi> tree, to practise sorcery, to love murder; <hi rend="bold">all these things </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="bold">(indeed)</hi></seg><hi rend="bold"> we forbid to every Christian on God's behalf.</hi>
crib.IICn_6|II 5–9: <hi rend="spaced">Secret</hi> killers, perjurers, violators of holy orders <seg type="recension">(and)</seg> of married wedlock, <hi rend="spaced">whom</hi> <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">ǽþbrece</hi> [adulterers], let them either <hi rend="bold">quickly</hi> <hi rend="spaced">run</hi> to penance or <hi rend="bold">hastily</hi> depart with <hi rend="spaced">their</hi> sins from our kingdom.
crib.IICn_7|II 5–9: Flatterers, liars, despoilers <hi rend="spaced">of the poor</hi> and robbers shall <hi rend="spaced">quickly</hi> incur the wrath of God, unless they <hi rend="spaced">come to their senses and cease and to God</hi> make amends.
crib.IICn_8|II 5–9: Let us all strive with all urgency to establish peace and security and <hi rend="spaced">stability</hi> of the coinage: peace and security such that it may benefit <hi rend="spaced">poor men</hi> and harm thieves; stability of the coinage such that one [coinage] <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">be held</hi> and)</seg> go throughout the whole land <hi rend="spaced">of England</hi> without falsity, which no one may reject.
crib.IICn_8-1|II 5–9: And whoever henceforth <hi rend="spaced">shall be found</hi> to have made false [coin], let him lose the hands with which he made the false, and let him redeem them with no money, neither with gold nor with silver.
crib.IICn_8-2|II 5–9: And if the <hi rend="spaced">sheriff</hi> <seg type="recension">(that is, the reeve <hi rend="spaced">of the town or vill</hi>)</seg> is accused that <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">the counterfeiter</hi>)</seg> did <hi rend="spaced">what he did</hi> by his licence, let him clear himself with threefold purgation, <hi rend="bold">of oath or of hot iron </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="bold">(that is, ordeal)</hi></seg><hi rend="bold">,</hi> which the English <hi rend="spaced">name</hi> <hi rend="italic">thrifealde lade</hi> [threefold exculpation] <seg type="recension">(with a purgation which the E. <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">þrefeald l.</hi>, <hi rend="bold">of o. or of h. i.,</hi> which the E. <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">ordel</hi>)</hi></seg><hi rend="bold">;</hi> and if he fails in the purgation, let him suffer what the <hi rend="spaced">false moneyer</hi> suffered.
crib.IICn_9|II 5–9: Measures and weights <hi rend="spaced">throughout the whole</hi> kingdom <hi rend="spaced">of England</hi> shall be so corrected that they be right <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="bold">uniform</hi>)</seg>.
crib.IICn_12|II 12–15.1a: These are the rights of the <hi rend="spaced">king</hi> which he has over all men in Wessex: the forfeiture <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">mundbrece</hi> [breach of protection], <hi rend="italic">hamsocne</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">that</hi> is, attack <hi rend="spaced">in one's own house or within the courtyard</hi> for the sake <hi rend="spaced">of some evil</hi>, <hi rend="italic">foresteal</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">which we can call 'obstruction'</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">for the sake of evil</hi>; <hi rend="italic">ferdƿite</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">which we can call 'desertion of the army'</hi>; these are, <hi rend="spaced">I say</hi>, the king's rights, unless the king wishes to <hi rend="spaced">honour</hi> someone by giving him <hi rend="spaced">what is of his right</hi>.
crib.IICn_13|II 12–15.1a: If anyone <hi rend="spaced">does</hi> the work of an outlaw, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">útlages ƿeorc</hi>, let the king see to [his] peace.
crib.IICn_13-1|II 12–15.1a: But if he has allodial land <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="italic">bocland</hi>)</seg>, let <seg type="recension">(his)</seg> <hi rend="spaced">whole</hi> be the king's, whosesoever man he be.
crib.IICn_13-2|II 12–15.1a: And whoever has fed an exile <seg type="recension">(whom the English <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">utlaga</hi></hi>)</seg> after the ex<hi rend="spaced">pulsion, which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">fede oþþe fermie</hi> [feeds or harbours], let him give the king <hi rend="spaced">a hundred shillings</hi>, unless he clears himself [by oath] that he did not know him [to be] expelled <hi rend="bold">[and] proclaimed, which the English call <hi rend="italic">gecydne utlage</hi> [declared outlaw].</hi>
crib.IICn_14|II 12–15.1a: In the Mercian law the king has the same <hi rend="spaced">rights</hi>.
crib.IICn_15|II 12–15.1a: But in the law of the Danes the king has these <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">rights</hi>)</seg>: violation <hi rend="bold">of the coinage,</hi> <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">feohƿíte</hi>,</hi> <hi rend="spaced">desertion of the army</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">ferdƿite</hi>, breach of the peace, <hi rend="spaced">which they call</hi> <hi rend="italic">griðbrece</hi>, attack in a house or in a <hi rend="spaced">courtyard, which they call <hi rend="italic">hamsocne</hi></hi>, unless <hi rend="spaced">the king wishes</hi> <hi rend="spaced">to give what is his</hi>.
crib.IICn_15-1|II 12–15.1a: If anyone devises unjust laws and judges [by them], either for the sake of hatred or of acquiring money, let him be liable to the king for <hi rend="bold">40</hi> shillings in the law of the English, unless he affirms by oath that he did not know how <hi rend="spaced">to judge</hi> more rightly, and afterwards let him lose his <hi rend="spaced">noble rank</hi>, unless he redeem it from the king at <hi rend="spaced">the king's will</hi>.
crib.IICn_15-1a|II 12–15.1a: In the law of the Danes he shall be liable for the forfeiture <hi rend="spaced">which</hi> <hi rend="bold">the Danes</hi> <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">lahslit</hi> [fine for breach of law] . . .
crib.InCn_II-15-1b|II 15.1b: In their law they call the <hi rend="italic">lahslit</hi> [fine for breach of law] of a free man of rank (thegn) ten half-marks, that is five marks; of a man having allodial land <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="italic">bocland</hi>)</seg> six half-marks, that is three marks; the <hi rend="italic">lahslit</hi> of a villein, whom the English call <hi rend="italic">ceorlman</hi>, twelve ores.
crib.IICn_15a|II 15.2–37: Whoever feeds an expelled man or <hi rend="spaced">keeps [him] peaceably</hi>, whom the English <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">friðleasne man</hi> [man without peace], let him pay the king, as the law is, <hi rend="spaced">full compensation</hi>, <hi rend="bold">and to him who expelled the expelled man his contempt-fine, if that is just.</hi>
crib.IICn_15-2|II 15.2–37: Whoever refuses right judgment and just law, let him be forfeit to the one to whom <hi rend="spaced">it is due</hi>: if to the king, let him give him <hi rend="bold">40</hi> shillings, if to the earl <hi rend="bold">20</hi> shillings, if to the hundred <hi rend="bold">10</hi> shillings, if against all these, <hi rend="spaced">let him pay to all</hi>.
crib.IICn_15-3|II 15.2–37: By the law of the Danes let him pay <hi rend="italic">lahslit</hi>.
crib.IICn_16|II 15.2–37: If anyone accuses another unjustly, <hi rend="spaced">so that the accused would lose through the denunciation</hi> of the accuser money or <hi rend="bold">life,</hi> <hi rend="spaced">and the accused</hi> clears <hi rend="spaced">himself</hi> of it, let the <hi rend="spaced">denouncer</hi> be liable for his tongue, unless he <hi rend="spaced">pays for the denounced</hi> according to his own price, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">say</hi>)</seg> <hi rend="italic">be his ƿere</hi> [by his wergeld].
crib.IICn_17|II 15.2–37: <hi rend="spaced">Let</hi> <hi rend="bold">popular</hi> courts <hi rend="spaced">be established</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">hundred</hi>, as <hi rend="bold">is just and has been done before this,</hi> under the forfeiture <hi rend="bold">which the law teaches;</hi> and let no one apply to the king unless he cannot obtain right in his hundred.
crib.IICn_18|II 15.2–37: Let civil courts be held three times a year, and the shire (court) <hi rend="spaced">be assembled</hi> twice a year, unless more be <hi rend="bold">necessary</hi>.
crib.IICn_18-1|II 15.2–37: And at that <hi rend="spaced">shire court</hi> let there be the bishop and the earl, who are to <hi rend="spaced">show</hi> the people both the justices of God and the rights of the world.
crib.IICn_19|II 15.2–37: <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">náme</hi> [distraint] neither within the shire nor outside, before he has three times sought justice in the hundred. Let no one take for any forfeiture anything which the English
crib.IICn_19-1|II 15.2–37: But if the third time he cannot have right, let him go to the shire (court) <hi rend="bold">and show that he has now gone to the hundred three times, sought right and could not have it;</hi> then let the shire appoint him a day, <hi rend="bold">on which he who is accused shall do right.</hi>
crib.IICn_19-2|II 15.2–37: But if <hi rend="spaced">the appointed day</hi> is broken, leave having been received from the shire for <hi rend="spaced">going</hi> and returning, so that he may <hi rend="bold">take <hi rend="italic">náme</hi>,</hi> until he has his own.
crib.IICn_20|II 15.2–37: We also establish that every free man who wishes to be worthy of <hi rend="spaced">exculpation and freedom</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">which</hi> <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">say</hi>)</seg> <hi rend="italic">lade þurþe ⁊ þeres þurþe</hi> [worthy of exculpation and of wergeld], be in a hundred and in <hi rend="bold">pledge;</hi> otherwise, if he is <hi rend="bold">slain</hi> after he is twelve years old, he shall be worthy of no freeman's status.
crib.IICn_20a|II 15.2–37: <hi rend="spaced">This too we say</hi> both of those who have house and <hi rend="spaced">land</hi> and of those who <hi rend="spaced">do not</hi>, but <hi rend="spaced">serve</hi> others, whom the English <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">husfæst ⁊ folgæres</hi> [householders and followers], that all be in a hundred and under pledge, which shall have <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">hold</hi>)</seg> them to justice, <hi rend="bold">if at any time they are accused of any matter.</hi>
crib.IICn_20-1|II 15.2–37: Many powerful men wish <hi rend="spaced">with</hi> <hi rend="spaced">cunning</hi> to defend in the cou<hi rend="spaced">rts their dependants</hi>, in whatever way seems to them easier to be able, for slaves or for free men; but we do not wish to consent to this injustice.
crib.IICn_21|II 15.2–37: <hi rend="spaced">Therefore</hi> we command that every man over <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">the age</hi>)</seg> of twelve years take an oath that he will neither be a thief nor be an accomplice of a thief.
crib.IICn_22|II 15.2–37: But if there is any trustworthy man, who has not <hi rend="spaced">rightly</hi> been accused <hi rend="spaced">of any shameful</hi> matter, and for whom neither the oath has broken in his mouth nor the ordeal <hi rend="bold">of iron or water,</hi> which <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">say</hi>)</seg> þa<hi rend="italic">m</hi> þe ue bærst ne aþ ne ordel [for whom neither oath nor ordeal has failed], <hi rend="spaced">such a one, if at any time he is accused, let him clear himself with simple</hi> purgation.
crib.IICn_22-1|II 15.2–37: But for an untrustworthy man let a [selected] oath be chosen, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">anfealdne að</hi> [single oath], in the hundred, and a threefold oath, as <hi rend="spaced">befits that court to which he belongs</hi>; or let him go to the ordeal.
crib.IICn_22-1a|II 15.2–37: But whoever must obtain simple purgation, let him <hi rend="spaced">do this</hi> with a simple oath, <hi rend="bold">that is, let him take two, and be himself the third, and so obtain it by swearing.</hi> <hi rend="bold">But a threefold oath is to be obtained thus: let him take five and be himself the sixth, and so by swearing acquire threefold ordeal or threefold oath.</hi>
crib.IICn_22-2|II 15.2–37: If a free man of rank (thegn), that is <hi rend="italic">þegen</hi>, has a trustworthy man <hi rend="spaced">who can swear the fore-oath for him</hi> <seg type="recension">(that is <hi rend="italic">foraþ</hi>)</seg>, so be it; but if he does not have one, let him <hi rend="spaced">swear</hi> himself.
crib.IICn_22-3|II 15.2–37: Nor shall any fore-oath be remitted to him.
crib.IICn_23|II 15.2–37: <hi rend="bold">If stolen goods are found in the hand or in the power of anyone who cannot excuse himself, if he wishes</hi> to name a warrantor, it shall in no way be allowed him, unless he has <hi rend="bold">two</hi> suitable witnesses who <hi rend="spaced">were seeing and hearing</hi> whence there came to him what was taken <hi rend="spaced">in his hand or in his power</hi>.
crib.IICn_23-1|II 15.2–37: And let the witnesses show this <hi rend="spaced">by oath</hi>, that they are rightly witnesses for him and <hi rend="spaced">trustworthy</hi>, as seeing and hearing, in the faith of God and by the faith <hi rend="spaced">of their lord</hi>, that he acquired it rightly.
crib.IICn_24|II 15.2–37: <hi rend="spaced">We wish</hi> also that no one buy anything above four pe<hi rend="spaced">nce in value</hi>, neither a living thing nor a <hi rend="spaced">dead</hi> one nor a lying one, without four suitable witnesses, neither within a borough nor <hi rend="spaced">outside</hi>.
crib.IICn_24-1|II 15.2–37: And if he does not have <hi rend="spaced">so many nor such</hi> witnesses, and some such thing is found <hi rend="spaced">in the hand</hi> or <hi rend="spaced">his power</hi>, and he <hi rend="spaced">wishes to vouch</hi> a warrantor, it shall not avail him <hi rend="spaced">nor</hi> be allowed, but let what is his be returned to the claimant — <hi rend="bold">or its value</hi> — and besides again as much in value, and the forfeiture [to him] who <hi rend="spaced">rightly</hi> ought to have it.
crib.IICn_24-2|II 15.2–37: But if he has <hi rend="spaced">such witnesses</hi> as we said above, let him vouch the warrantor; <hi rend="bold">and let the one vouched vouch another, if he can, and the third further vouch a third, if he can;</hi> and the third shall make it his own, <hi rend="spaced">if he is able; but if he is not able</hi>, let it be returned to him who rightly ought to have it.
crib.IICn_24-3|II 15.2–37: To us <hi rend="spaced">however</hi> it seems unjust that anyone should claim for himself <hi rend="spaced">by swearing</hi> <hi rend="spaced">what is rightly his</hi>, where there are witnesses, and at least before six months after <hi rend="spaced">what he seeks</hi> was taken away by theft.
crib.IICn_25|II 15.2–37: Whoever has often been accused of theft and, summoned [to] the <hi rend="bold">hundred</hi>, three times declines: let men be found from the <hi rend="bold">hundred</hi> who shall go to him; and let him find, if he can, sureties still.
crib.IICn_25a|II 15.2–37: But if he <hi rend="spaced">could not or would not</hi>, let him be taken either alive or dead, and all that he has.
crib.IICn_25-1|II 15.2–37: And <hi rend="spaced">first</hi> let there be returned to the claimant from the thief's goods [what] <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">his ceapgeld</hi> [his purchase-price]; and what remains <hi rend="spaced">let be divided</hi> in half between the hundred and the lord <hi rend="spaced">of the thief</hi>.
crib.IICn_25-2|II 15.2–37: But if a kinsman <hi rend="spaced">of that thief or anyone else</hi> refuses to go against <hi rend="spaced">that</hi> thief, as <hi rend="spaced">we have said</hi>, let him give the king <hi rend="bold">40</hi> shillings.
crib.IICn_26|II 15.2–37: A public thief and betrayer of his own lord, <hi rend="spaced">whom the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">hlaford</hi><hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">spice</hi></hi> [lord-traitor], whatever they re<hi rend="spaced">quest, let them nowhere find life</hi>.
crib.IICn_27|II 15.2–37: If anyone in the courts wishes to defend himself or his man by counter-accusations, let those accusations be held as nothing, but <hi rend="spaced">let him answer the one accusing him</hi>, as the <hi rend="italic">hundred</hi> shall judge.
crib.IICn_28|II 15.2–37: Let no one keep any man longer than <hi rend="spaced">three nights</hi>, unless <hi rend="spaced">his lord</hi>, whom he served before, has commended him. <hi rend="bold">But if he does otherwise, let him pay the former lord his contempt-fine and the king his forfeiture.</hi>
crib.IICn_28-1|II 15.2–37: Let no one put away from himself his servant before he is cleared of every accusation of which he was previously accused.
crib.IICn_29|II 15.2–37: If a thief encounters anyone, and he willingly lets him go without hue and cry, let him pay for the thief, <hi rend="bold">to whom it is due,</hi> at the price of the same thief, or let him clear himself with a full oath that he <hi rend="spaced">did not know him to be a thief</hi>.
crib.IICn_30|II 15.2–37: If anyone is untrustworthy to his hundred and is often accused, if he is charged <hi rend="spaced">together on one day with three accusations</hi>, let him <hi rend="spaced">clear himself</hi> by threefold ordeal.
crib.IICn_30-1|II 15.2–37: But if his lord says that <hi rend="spaced">never for him</hi> has oath <seg type="recension">(sworn oath)</seg> or ordeal broken, nor has he paid the price of theft, then let that lord take with him two trustworthy men and <hi rend="spaced">affirm by oath that it is so</hi>, unless he has such a reeve as is worthy <hi rend="spaced">to do this same for him</hi>.
crib.IICn_30-2|II 15.2–37: If the oath goes well, let <hi rend="spaced">the accused choose</hi> which of these he wishes, either simple ordeal or an oath <hi rend="bold">of 20 shillings</hi> in three hundreds, above 30 pence.
crib.IICn_30-3|II 15.2–37: But if they <hi rend="spaced">dare</hi> not make the oath, let him go to the threefold ordeal.
crib.IICn_30-3a|II 15.2–37: Thus <hi rend="spaced">is to be obtained</hi> that threefold ordeal <seg type="recension">(which <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> ‘<hi rend="bold">ofræce</hi> <hi rend="italic">þæt</hi> ordel')</seg>: let him take with him five and be himself the sixth; <hi rend="spaced">for thus</hi> is threefold ordeal obtained.
crib.IICn_30-3b|II 15.2–37: But if he is guilty and <hi rend="spaced">fails</hi> in the ordeal, the first time let him before other things repay <hi rend="spaced">the accusers</hi> double what is theirs, and to their lords <hi rend="spaced">their price</hi>, and afterwards let them <hi rend="spaced">find</hi> sureties that they will thenceforth <hi rend="spaced">desist</hi>.
crib.IICn_30-4|II 15.2–37: If they <hi rend="spaced">fail</hi> a second time, let their hands or feet be cut off, <hi rend="spaced">or both, if the guilt be so great</hi>.
crib.IICn_30-5|II 15.2–37: But if he has done still greater things, let his eyes be put out, and his nose be taken off with the lip, and the ears, or the skin of the head with the hair, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">behætian</hi></hi> [to scalp]; thus can <hi rend="spaced">thieves</hi> be corrected and <hi rend="spaced">souls</hi> saved.
crib.IICn_30-6|II 15.2–37: But if the <hi rend="spaced">accused escapes</hi> and avoids the ordeal, the sureties are to <hi rend="spaced">pay back to the accuser</hi> what he claimed from the <hi rend="spaced">thief</hi>, and to the king the price of the <hi rend="spaced">thief</hi>, or to him who has <hi rend="bold">sake and soke.</hi>
crib.IICn_30-7|II 15.2–37: But if the lord of the thief is accused, as though he willingly <hi rend="spaced">let</hi> him go, taking five <hi rend="spaced">trustworthy men</hi> let him clear himself, <hi rend="spaced">if he can</hi>.
crib.IICn_30-8|II 15.2–37: If he clears himself, let there be given to him the <hi rend="spaced">price of the thief, that is,</hi> the <hi rend="italic">ƿere</hi>.
crib.IICn_30-9|II 15.2–37: If he cannot <hi rend="spaced">clear</hi> himself, let the king have that price; and let the thief be held <hi rend="spaced">an outlaw and guilty</hi> by all the people.
crib.IICn_31|II 15.2–37: Every lord is to have his household in his own <seg type="recension">(his)</seg> pledge, so that, if any <hi rend="spaced">of them</hi> is accused, he answers to the <hi rend="italic">hundred</hi> in which he is accused, as is right.
crib.IICn_31-1|II 15.2–37: If he escapes <hi rend="spaced">after</hi> the accusation, the lord is to pay his <hi rend="italic">ƿere</hi> to the king, <hi rend="bold">and to the pledges what he was accused of. But if within a year and a day his lord can catch him, he is to get back what he gave for him.</hi>
crib.IICn_31-1a|II 15.2–37: And if the lord himself is accused of having let him flee willingly, <hi rend="bold">if he is a free man of rank,</hi> that <hi rend="spaced">is a <hi rend="italic">þegen</hi></hi> [thegn], taking five of his like let him clear himself.
crib.IICn_31-2|II 15.2–37: If he <hi rend="spaced">cannot</hi> clear himself, let him pay the king his <hi rend="italic">ƿere</hi>; and the man is to be an outlaw <hi rend="spaced">from all</hi>.
crib.IICn_32|II 15.2–37: If a <hi rend="spaced">slave fails</hi> in the ordeal <hi rend="bold">of iron or water,</hi> a mark <hi rend="spaced">of crime</hi> is to be made on him the first time.
crib.IICn_32-1|II 15.2–37: If he fails a second time, let nothing else be accepted <hi rend="spaced">by way of amends</hi>, except that his head <hi rend="spaced">be cut off</hi>.
crib.IICn_33|II 15.2–37: Whoever is untrustworthy to all the people, the king's reeve is to put him under sureties, so that they keep him to justice.
crib.IICn_33-1|II 15.2–37: And if he <hi rend="spaced">cannot</hi> have pledges, let him be killed and buried in the place of thieves.
crib.IICn_33-1a|II 15.2–37: But if perhaps anyone wishes to defend him by force, let him have the same law.
crib.IICn_33-2|II 15.2–37: And whoever neglects these things and will not do them, as we all together <hi rend="spaced">agreed</hi>, let him give the king <hi rend="bold">forty</hi> shillings.
crib.IICn_34|II 15.2–37: And let there be among <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">all</hi>)</seg> the towns one law and one purgation.
crib.IICn_35|II 15.2–37: If a stranger or foreigner, who comes from afar, is in difficulty for lack of friends, so that he cannot have pledges, at the first accusation, then let him undergo the <hi rend="bold">king's</hi> custody and wait there until he goes to the ordeal <hi rend="bold">of iron or water</hi> and there find what he can.
crib.IICn_35-1|II 15.2–37: <hi rend="spaced">Truly I tell you</hi>, if anyone judges a <hi rend="spaced">different</hi> judgement for a stranger or foreigner coming from afar, he harms himself.
crib.IICn_36|II 15.2–37: If anyone commits perjury <hi rend="bold">on the text of the Gospel or</hi> on the relics of the saints and is convicted <hi rend="spaced">of having sworn unjustly</hi>, let him lose his <hi rend="spaced">hands</hi> or give half of his own price; and this is to be divided between the bishop and the lord of that man.
crib.IICn_36-1|II 15.2–37: And after this let him not be worthy of an oath, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">aðes þyrðe</hi>, unless he makes satisfaction to God more deeply and finds sureties that he will cease henceforth.
crib.IICn_37|II 15.2–37: But whoever stands in false witness and is convicted <hi rend="spaced">that</hi> it is so, let him no longer be worthy to stand or <hi rend="spaced">bear witness</hi>, <hi rend="bold">because he has lost his lawfulness</hi>, and therefore let him pay to the king or to the lord of the land <hi rend="bold">X shillings,</hi> which the <hi rend="bold">Danes</hi> <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">halsfang</hi>.
crib.IICn_39|II 39–42: If anyone kills <hi rend="spaced">one of the</hi> servants of the altar, let him be an outlaw before God and before <hi rend="spaced">all</hi> men, unless he makes amends more deeply through exile, and to the kinsmen also; or let him clear himself with the purgation <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">ƿerelade</hi>.
crib.IICn_39-1|II 39–42: And within thirty days let him begin penance and amends towards God and men.
crib.IICn_40|II 39–42: If anyone through his counsel causes a man in orders or a stranger to lose money or life, then the king must be to him for kinsman and for <hi rend="spaced">lord</hi>, unless he has another.
crib.IICn_40-1|II 39–42: And let amends be made to the king according to what is right, or let the king himself strictly avenge <hi rend="spaced">what has been done</hi>,
crib.IICn_40-2|II 39–42: <hi rend="spaced">because</hi> it befits and becomes a Christian king that he sharply take vengeance on <hi rend="spaced">those who violate the laws of God</hi>.
crib.IICn_41|II 39–42: If a minister of the altar commits homicide or some great crime, let him lose both his order and his <hi rend="spaced">rank</hi> and go into exile, according to what the pope appoints for him.
crib.IICn_41-1|II 39–42: But if he wishes to clear himself, let him clear himself with a threefold <hi rend="spaced">oath</hi>.
crib.IICn_41-2|II 39–42: And unless within thirty days he has begun amends and to both God and <hi rend="spaced">men made satisfaction, let him be driven from the land</hi> and be an outlaw.
crib.IICn_42|II 39–42: If anyone binds or beats or shamefully mocks someone in orders, let him make amends to him according to what is right — <hi rend="bold">namely according to the measure of his order</hi> —, and to the bishop the altar-amends, <hi rend="spaced">which is called</hi> <hi rend="italic">þeofodbote</hi>, and to the lord or the king the full contempt-fine, <hi rend="spaced">all these</hi> according to the measure of the order; or let him clear himself with full purgation.
crib.IICn_44|II 44–50.1: If a thief <hi rend="spaced">or another</hi> condemned to death seeks confession, let it in no way be denied him.
crib.IICn_44-1|II 44–50.1: But if <hi rend="spaced">anyone does so</hi>, let him make amends to the king; or clear himself as one of six.
crib.IICn_45|II 44–50.1: Let no <hi rend="spaced">thief or</hi> man condemned to death be killed on the Lord's day <hi rend="bold">or on any other feast day</hi>, unless he <hi rend="spaced">wishes</hi> to flee or fight; but let him be guarded until the feast passes.
crib.IICn_45-1|II 44–50.1: If a free man works on a feast day and <hi rend="spaced">so violates the feast</hi>, let him pay <hi rend="bold">ten shillings</hi>, and nonetheless make satisfaction to God.
crib.IICn_45-2|II 44–50.1: If a slave <hi rend="spaced">does this</hi>, let him lose his hide or make amends according to the measure of the deed.
crib.IICn_45-3|II 44–50.1: But if he did this <hi rend="spaced">unwilling</hi>, at his lord's <hi rend="spaced">command</hi>, let the lord lose that slave and give <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">halsfang</hi>;</hi> and let the slave be wholly free; or let the lord clear himself.
crib.IICn_46|II 44–50.1: If a free man breaks a fast, according to the Danes let him pay <hi rend="italic">lahslit</hi> <seg type="recension"><hi rend="bold">(that is, X shillings)</hi></seg>, according to the English by the nature <hi rend="spaced">of the fast</hi>.
crib.IICn_46-1|II 44–50.1: If a <hi rend="spaced">slave</hi> breaks a fast by eating meat, let him be beaten according to the measure of the fault.
crib.IICn_47|II 44–50.1: If anyone violates the Lenten fast either by fighting or by robbing or by <hi rend="spaced">marrying</hi> a woman or by doing some great evil, let him make double amends according to the amends for the deed of a <hi rend="spaced">violated</hi> feast.
crib.IICn_47-1|II 44–50.1: And <hi rend="spaced">if he denies it</hi>, let him deny it with a threefold purgation.
crib.IICn_48|II 44–50.1: If anyone defends any of the church's rights with arms, let him make amends of <hi rend="bold">ten shillings</hi> according to the Danes; if he denies it, let him take eleven and himself be the twelfth and <hi rend="spaced">so clear himself</hi>.
crib.IICn_48-1|II 44–50.1: But if he wounds <hi rend="spaced">anyone</hi> there, let him make amends for it <hi rend="spaced">to him</hi> on whom he inflicted the <hi rend="spaced">wound</hi>, and to the lord <hi rend="spaced">of that man the full</hi> forfeiture, and let him redeem <hi rend="spaced">his hand</hi> from the bishop or lose it.
crib.IICn_48-2|II 44–50.1: And if he kills a man, let him be an outlaw and be driven out with hue and cry <hi rend="spaced">by all</hi> <hi rend="spaced">who</hi> want <hi rend="spaced">God's justice</hi>.
crib.IICn_48-3|II 44–50.1: And if <hi rend="spaced">he himself</hi> is killed, <hi rend="spaced">for the reason</hi> that he fought against justice, let him lie unpaid for, <hi rend="spaced">which the English say</hi> <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">call</hi>)</seg> <hi rend="italic">ægylde</hi>.
crib.IICn_49|II 44–50.1: Whoever violates holy orders, <hi rend="bold">as when he beats either a monk or a priest or anyone in orders or does anything of this kind,</hi> let him make amends for these things thus according to the measure of <hi rend="spaced">the order of the injured party</hi>: either according to the price, that is <hi rend="italic">þere</hi>, or according to the forfeiture, or according to all that the <hi rend="spaced">wrongdoer</hi> has.
crib.IICn_50-1|II 44–50.1: If anyone violates marriage, <hi rend="bold">namely while lying under [i.e. bound to] his own wife,</hi> and fornicates with <hi rend="spaced">another woman</hi> or, what is worse, with another man's wife, let him do penance <hi rend="bold">according to the penitential book.</hi>
crib.IICn_52|II 52: [52] A widow <hi rend="spaced">also</hi>, if she is carried off by force, and intercourse has been had with her, let it be paid for with a <hi rend="bold">like</hi> price.
crib.IICn_52-1|II 52: [52, 1] If anyone carries off a virgin by force and lies with her, let him pay for her with her price, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> be <hi rend="bold">hyre</hi> <hi rend="italic">þere</hi>.
crib.IICn_52-1|II 52a: [52, 1] If anyone carries off a virgin by force and lies with her, let him pay for her with her price, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> be <hi rend="bold">hyre</hi> <hi rend="italic">þere</hi>.
crib.IICn_53|II 53–59: A woman who, while her husband is living, commits adultery with another man, and it is made public, let her become for herself a disgrace before the world, and let her lawful husband have all her property; but let her lose nose and ears.
crib.IICn_53-1|II 53–59: But if she <hi rend="spaced">denies</hi> it and <hi rend="spaced">wishes to clear herself</hi>, and fails in the <hi rend="bold">ordeal</hi>, let the bishop <hi rend="spaced">look into it</hi> and judge strictly.
crib.IICn_54|II 53–59: If a man having a lawful wife fornicates with his slave-woman, let him lose that slave-woman and make amends for himself to God and men.
crib.IICn_54-1|II 53–59: Whoever has a lawful wife and also a concubine, let no priest <hi rend="bold">nor anyone else</hi> do him any service that ought to be done for a Christian, until he has desisted.
crib.IICn_55|II 53–59: If foreigners do not <hi rend="spaced">keep</hi> <hi rend="spaced">lawful</hi> marriage, let them be expelled from the land with their goods and sins.
crib.IICn_56|II 53–59: If there is open murder, so that someone is killed <hi rend="spaced">by it</hi>, let him be handed over to his kinsmen.
crib.IICn_56-1|II 53–59: And if <hi rend="spaced">a purgation</hi> comes about, and he fails in the purgation, let the bishop <hi rend="spaced">see and judge</hi>.
crib.IICn_57|II 53–59: Whoever plots treachery against the king or his lord, let him lose all his goods and be guilty of death, unless he <hi rend="spaced">clears</hi> himself by a threefold ordeal.
crib.IICn_58|II 53–59: If anyone breaks the king's pledge, let him make amends with five pounds.
crib.IICn_58-1|II 53–59: And whoever breaks the pledge of an archbishop or of a prince, <hi rend="spaced">whom the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">æðeling</hi>, let him make amends with III pounds;
crib.IICn_58-2|II 53–59: of a bishop or an earl, let him make amends with II pounds.
crib.IICn_59|II 53–59: If anyone fights in the <seg type="recension">(royal)</seg> hall of the king, let him lose his life, unless the king wishes to spare him. . . .
crib.Af_15|II 59a; b; c: . . . . Whoever fights or draws weapons before the archbishop, let him make amends with <hi rend="bold">forty</hi> shillings; <hi rend="spaced">and</hi> whoever <hi rend="spaced">does</hi> this before a bishop or an earl, let him make amends with <hi rend="bold">twenty</hi> shillings.
crib.Af_16|II 59a; b; c: If anyone <hi rend="spaced">steals</hi> a cow or a mare, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call <hi rend="italic">stodmere</hi></hi>, and a calf or a foal <hi rend="spaced">with them, let him pay for the foal</hi> <hi rend="bold">with twelve pence</hi> <hi rend="spaced">and for the calf likewise</hi> and for the mothers according to their price.
crib.Af_17|II 59a; b; c: If anyone entrusts <hi rend="spaced">some</hi> <hi rend="spaced">man to another man</hi> <hi rend="bold">not a kinsman</hi>, and the <hi rend="spaced">entrusted man himself perishes while in that keeping</hi>, and someone accuses him <hi rend="spaced">that through his treachery</hi> he <hi rend="spaced">perished</hi>, let him clear himself . . . .
crib.Af_38|II 59d; e; f; g; h; i: If anyone fights before the earl at a court meeting, let him make amends according to the price <hi rend="bold">of himself</hi> and the forfeiture, <hi rend="spaced">which</hi> <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">ƿer</hi> ⁊ <hi rend="italic">ƿite</hi>; and before this let him <hi rend="spaced">pay</hi> the earl <hi rend="bold">XL</hi> shillings.
crib.Af_38-1|II 59d; e; f; g; h; i: <hi rend="spaced">And if</hi> he stirs up <hi rend="spaced">the assembly</hi> of the people by drawing <hi rend="spaced">his</hi> weapons, let him <hi rend="spaced">pay</hi> the earl <hi rend="bold">XL</hi> shillings.
crib.Af_38-2|II 59d; e; f; g; h; i: But if such a thing is done before the <hi rend="bold">sheriff</hi> or before the king's chaplain, let him <hi rend="spaced">make amends</hi> with XXX shillings.
crib.Af_39|II 59d; e; f; g; h; i: If anyone <hi rend="spaced">starts</hi> a fight <hi rend="bold">in the earl's hall, let him make amends with XX shillings</hi>, and if <hi rend="bold">this happens</hi> in the house of a man <hi rend="spaced">whom the English call</hi> ceorl<hi rend="bold">man</hi> <seg type="recension">(or <hi rend="bold">ceorlboren</hi>)</seg>, let him <hi rend="spaced">make amends</hi> to him with VI shillings.
crib.Af_39-1|II 59d; e; f; g; h; i: If he draws weapons and does not fight, let him <hi rend="spaced">make amends</hi> with III shillings.
crib.Af_39-2|II 59d; e; f; g; h; i: <hi rend="spaced">But if this happens in the house of a man</hi> <hi rend="bold">whom the English name</hi> <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">radcniht</hi>,</hi> but others <hi rend="italic">sexhende</hi><hi rend="bold">man</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">three times</hi> <hi rend="spaced">more dearly</hi> <hi rend="spaced">let amends be made to him</hi>, <hi rend="bold">that is XVIII shillings</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">than to him</hi> <hi rend="bold">whom we named above <hi rend="italic">ceorlman</hi>.</hi> If <hi rend="spaced">in the house</hi> <hi rend="bold">of a man of rank, whom we named above thegen,</hi> <hi rend="spaced">and whom</hi> <hi rend="spaced">some</hi> <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> twelfhende<hi rend="bold">man</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">this happens</hi>, doubly <hi rend="spaced">let amends be made</hi> to him, more than to him <hi rend="spaced">whom</hi> <hi rend="bold">we named</hi> <hi rend="italic">sexhende</hi><hi rend="bold">man</hi>, <hi rend="bold">that is XXXVI shillings</hi> . . . .
crib.IICn_60|II 60–66: . . . If anyone disarms a man against justice, let him make amends to him with <hi rend="bold">X shillings</hi>; and if he is bound, let half his price, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> be healue <hi rend="italic">þere</hi>, be paid to him.
crib.IICn_61|II 60–66: If anyone breaks the peace <hi rend="spaced">in war</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">griþbrece</hi>, he is guilty of death or of his price.
crib.IICn_62|II 60–66: If anyone makes an attack on a house <hi rend="spaced">or</hi> a court, which <hi rend="spaced">the English</hi> <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">say</hi>)</seg> <hi rend="spaced">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">hamsocne</hi>, let him make amends to the king with five pounds.
crib.IICn_62-1|II 60–66: And if he is killed in that <hi rend="spaced">attack</hi>, let him lie unpaid for, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">ægelde</hi>.
crib.IICn_63|II 60–66: If anyone commits robbery, let him give back and pay compensation, and be liable for his price to the king.
crib.IICn_64|II 60–66: Destruction of a house and burning <hi rend="spaced">of it</hi> and <hi rend="spaced">a public thief</hi> and murder and <hi rend="spaced">a plotter against</hi> his own <hi rend="spaced">lord</hi> <seg type="recension">(traitor)</seg> <hi rend="spaced">go beyond</hi> all amends, nor do they have <hi rend="spaced">any</hi>.
crib.IICn_65|II 60–66: If anyone neglects the repair of a town or a bridge or going to <hi rend="spaced">war</hi>, let him pay the king <hi rend="bold">XL</hi> shillings; or let him clear himself thus: let fourteen be named for him, and let him obtain eleven and <hi rend="spaced">himself be the twelfth</hi>.
crib.IICn_66|II 60–66: If anyone unjustly harbours <hi rend="italic">Godes flyman</hi> [God's fugitive], let him deliver him to justice and pay the <hi rend="bold">contempt-fine</hi> to whom it is due; and to the king let him pay amends of his price, that <hi rend="spaced">is be</hi> <hi rend="italic">þere</hi>.
crib.IICn_66-1|II 60–66: If anyone keeps with him an excommunicate or a <hi rend="spaced">proclaimed</hi> outlaw, <hi rend="spaced">let him lose all</hi> his goods and his life, <hi rend="bold">unless the king spares him.</hi>
crib.IICn_69|II 69–80.1: This is the relief which I wish to be made for all the people, in which hitherto they have been burdened beyond measure.
crib.IICn_69-1|II 69–80.1: This is first: I command all my reeves that on my own <hi rend="bold">estates</hi> they plough well and <hi rend="spaced">fully</hi> and <hi rend="bold">sow and cultivate the fields excellently</hi> and from that feed me and <hi rend="spaced">mine</hi>, and from no one <hi rend="bold">unjustly extort</hi> anything with which they could <seg type="recension">(should)</seg> feed me, unless someone of his own accord and <hi rend="spaced">willingly</hi> wishes to offer them some help.
crib.IICn_69-2|II 69–80.1: But if anyone henceforth exacts any forfeiture from someone <hi rend="bold">who would not help them in this,</hi> let him <hi rend="spaced">pay</hi> his price, <hi rend="spaced">that is</hi> <hi rend="italic">þere</hi>, to the king.
crib.IICn_70|II 69–80.1: If anyone falls dumb <hi rend="spaced">before</hi> he goes out of this life, whether through negligence or through sudden death, let his lord not meddle at all with any of his goods, except as much as rightly <hi rend="spaced">belongs</hi> to him, <hi rend="spaced">that is, just what the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">heregeate</hi>.
crib.IICn_70-1|II 69–80.1: But let all his things <hi rend="spaced">be divided</hi> according to his disposition among wife and children and <hi rend="spaced">his</hi> kinsmen.
crib.IICn_71|II 69–80.1: And that due, which above we <hi rend="spaced">named</hi> <hi rend="italic">heregeat</hi>, let it be suitably prepared thus, according to what <hi rend="bold">he was born [to]:</hi>
crib.IICn_71a|II 69–80.1: Of an earl, as <hi rend="spaced">befits an earl</hi>, that is eight horses, IIII with saddles and four without saddles, IIII helmets and four mail-coats, eight lances and as many shields and <hi rend="bold">fifty</hi> mancuses of gold.
crib.IICn_71-2|II 69–80.1: Of a middling man, <hi rend="bold">whom the English call <hi rend="italic">læsseþegen</hi>,</hi> his <hi rend="spaced"><hi rend="italic">heregeat</hi></hi> is: a horse and arms or <hi rend="italic">halsfang</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">which is</hi> <hi rend="bold">X shillings,</hi> in þeassexe [Wessex]; in Mercia <hi rend="spaced">however</hi> and in Eastengle [East Anglia] two pounds <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">of pence</hi>)</seg>.
crib.IICn_71-3|II 69–80.1: Of a free man of rank (thegn) who has his customs, <hi rend="spaced">whom the English call</hi> kinges <hi rend="italic">þegen</hi>, the due <hi rend="spaced">after his death</hi>, which above we <hi rend="spaced">named</hi> <hi rend="italic">heregeat</hi>: IIII pounds;
crib.IICn_71-4|II 69–80.1: and, if he was known to the king: two horses, one with a saddle and the other without, one sword and two lances and two shields and fifty mancuses of gold;
crib.IICn_71-5|II 69–80.1: and he who cannot <seg type="recension">(has not or)</seg> [pay] so much: XL <hi rend="spaced">shillings</hi>.
crib.IICn_72|II 69–80.1: Where a <hi rend="spaced">man</hi> dies without any claim [against him], either concerning <hi rend="spaced">land</hi> <hi rend="bold">or concerning another thing,</hi> his wife and children shall remain <hi rend="spaced">likewise</hi> [undisturbed].
crib.IICn_72-1|II 69–80.1: But if the man before his death was <hi rend="spaced">accused of such things</hi>, it is necessary that <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="spaced">his</hi>)</seg> heirs answer according to <hi rend="spaced">justice</hi>, as he himself would have had to, if he were alive.
crib.IICn_73|II 69–80.1: And the widow shall remain without a husband for an entire year.
crib.IICn_73a|II 69–80.1: If she before the year does otherwise <seg type="recension">(marries)</seg>, she shall lose her dower and all the goods which she had through her first husband; and the nearest <hi rend="spaced">kinsmen of the former husband</hi> shall have the lands and <hi rend="spaced">all other things</hi> which she <hi rend="spaced">has justly lost</hi>.
crib.IICn_73-1|II 69–80.1: But the man afterwards accepted shall be liable for his own price [wergeld] to the king or to him to whom the king has granted this.
crib.IICn_73-2|II 69–80.1: And although she had been forced to <hi rend="spaced">accept him</hi>, unless she withdraws from him entirely, so that she never again becomes his, she shall lose <hi rend="spaced">all the above-mentioned</hi> goods.
crib.IICn_73-3|II 69–80.1: And yet we <hi rend="spaced">forbid</hi> that a widow be veiled too hastily.
crib.IICn_73-4|II 69–80.1: But she shall pay the due to her <hi rend="spaced">lord, which above</hi> we <hi rend="spaced">have named</hi> <hi rend="italic">heregeat</hi> [heriot], within twelve months, unless it is convenient for her earlier.
crib.IICn_74|II 69–80.1: Let no one force a woman or a <hi rend="spaced">maiden against their will</hi> to what displeases them, neither for money <hi rend="spaced">nor for any other thing</hi>, unless someone of his own accord wishes to give something.
crib.IICn_75|II 69–80.1: If anyone has set his lance at someone's door and has entered the house <hi rend="spaced">for some reason</hi>, or if somewhere he <hi rend="spaced">has found</hi> weapons lying in some <hi rend="spaced">secluded</hi> place, where they could be without harm if they were left alone, and he has put his lance there, and another seizes it from there and does some harm with it, then it is right that he himself who <hi rend="spaced">did harm with the lance</hi>, he himself make amends for the harm.
crib.IICn_75-1|II 69–80.1: And he who <hi rend="spaced">put the lance</hi> where it <hi rend="spaced">could have</hi> lain without <hi rend="spaced">injury</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">if it were left alone</hi>, shall clear himself, if he dares, that it was not by his will nor power nor counsel nor his witness that <hi rend="spaced">the harm which was done was done</hi>: it will then be right according to <hi rend="spaced">justice</hi> that he be blameless.
crib.IICn_75-2|II 69–80.1: And the wrongdoer shall make amends for the <hi rend="spaced">harm</hi> which he did, according as the law teaches.
crib.IICn_76|II 69–80.1: If anyone carries something <hi rend="spaced">stolen</hi> to his house, and it <hi rend="spaced">has been</hi> discovered, it is just that he have what he sought.
crib.IICn_76-1|II 69–80.1: And unless the <hi rend="spaced">stolen thing is found</hi> under the woman's keys, she shall be free [of guilt].
crib.IICn_76-1a|II 69–80.1: These <hi rend="spaced">keys</hi>, however, <hi rend="spaced">the woman</hi> must keep under her care, namely of her storeroom and her chest and her casket; under these <hi rend="spaced">keys, therefore,</hi> if it <hi rend="spaced">has not been found</hi>, the woman will be without blame.
crib.IICn_76-2|II 69–80.1: Until now there <hi rend="spaced">has been</hi> <hi rend="spaced">a certain</hi> <hi rend="spaced">wicked</hi> custom in <hi rend="spaced">this</hi> land, that children who lay in cradles, although they did not yet take any food, were judged by the greedy equally guilty, as if they had understanding.
crib.IICn_76-3|II 69–80.1: But I <hi rend="spaced">forbid</hi> this in every way, and many other things which are very contrary to God.
crib.IICn_77|II 69–80.1: If anyone, <hi rend="spaced">terrified</hi> by fear, flees from his lord or from <hi rend="spaced">his comrades</hi> out of battle, whether on land or on sea <seg type="recension">(water)</seg>, he shall lose all his goods along with his life; and the <seg type="recension">(his)</seg> lord shall take all things that are his, and the land, if he had given him any before.
crib.IICn_77-1|II 69–80.1: But if he has <hi rend="spaced">allodial land</hi>, it shall be the king's.
crib.IICn_78|II 69–80.1: But if anyone falls before his lord in battle, whether in the country or outside the country, <hi rend="spaced">his lord's due</hi>, namely <seg type="recension">(which we <hi rend="spaced">named above</hi>)</seg> <hi rend="italic">heregeat</hi> [heriot], shall be remitted <hi rend="bold">to his wife or heirs;</hi> and the heirs shall have all his things with the lands and divide them justly.
crib.IICn_79|II 69–80.1: Whoever has justly defended his land with the shire (court) as witness shall possess it without claim while he lives, and if it pleases him to sell or give it, let him give it to whomever he pleases.
crib.IICn_80|II 69–80.1: I will also that every man have his hunting in the woods and in the open country on his own [land].
crib.IICn_80-1|II 69–80.1: And let all avoid mine, wherever I wish to have it.
crib.IICn_82|II 82–83.2: We <hi rend="spaced">command</hi> also that every man have peace and security <hi rend="spaced">going</hi> and returning to the court, unless he is <hi rend="spaced">altogether</hi> a public thief.
crib.IICn_83|II 82–83.2: Whoever, be he English or Dane, violates these laws which the king has <hi rend="spaced">now granted to all men</hi> <hi rend="spaced">and established</hi>, shall pay to the king his own price.
crib.IICn_83-1|II 82–83.2: If a second time he <hi rend="spaced">does this same thing</hi>, he shall make amends doubly <hi rend="spaced">according to the above reckoning</hi>.
crib.IICn_83-2|II 82–83.2: But if <hi rend="spaced">daringly</hi> a third time he presumes this, he shall lose all his things. . . . . . .
crib.InCn_III-1|III 1: <hi rend="small">If anyone takes something <hi rend="spaced">for some forfeiture</hi> before he justly seeks right, he shall give back what he took and pay a second time; and</hi> <seg type="recension">(to the king)</seg> <hi rend="small">shall pay forty shillings</hi> <seg type="recension">(or to him)</seg> who has his sake and soke; and in addition his price to his lord.
crib.InCn_III-2|III 2: <hi rend="small">We call [them] thieves up to VII men; from seven to XXXV <hi rend="spaced">the English call [it]</hi> <hi rend="italic">hloth</hi> [band], from XXXV onward it will be an army.</hi>
crib.InCn_III-3|III 3: <hi rend="small">Whoever is accused of <hi rend="italic">hloth</hi> [band], if he denies it, shall clear himself thus:</hi> having taken eleven men, he himself being the twelfth; or he shall pay the accuser's contempt [fine] and give two pounds as forfeiture to him who has his customs.
crib.InCn_III-4|III 4: <hi rend="small">And if anyone is accused as though he led an army against someone, and he denies it, he shall clear himself according to the price</hi> of the accuser, or pay it.
crib.Af_29|III 5–8: If anyone through a <hi rend="italic">hloth</hi> [band] kills a man <hi rend="bold">whom</hi> <hi rend="bold">some</hi> <hi rend="bold">English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">tƿihende</hi> <hi rend="bold">and others <hi rend="italic">ceorlman</hi>,</hi> <hi rend="spaced">he who acknowledges that he killed him</hi> shall pay <hi rend="spaced">according to his</hi> <hi rend="italic">were</hi> [wergeld] <hi rend="spaced">and also render the forfeitures</hi>, and each of <hi rend="spaced">his companions who were then with him</hi> shall pay thirty shillings.
crib.Af_30|III 5–8: But if <hi rend="spaced">such a man is killed</hi> <hi rend="bold">as above</hi> <hi rend="bold">we have named <hi rend="italic">radcniht</hi></hi> <hi rend="bold">and some</hi> <hi rend="bold">English</hi> <hi rend="bold">call</hi> <hi rend="italic">sexhendeman</hi>, the slayer shall <hi rend="spaced">pay</hi> <hi rend="italic">ƿer</hi> [wergeld] and <hi rend="italic">wite</hi> [fine] and each <hi rend="spaced">of his companions</hi> LX shillings.
crib.Af_31|III 5–8: If he <hi rend="spaced">who was killed</hi> was <hi rend="bold">a free man of rank (thegn), that is <hi rend="italic">þegen</hi>,</hi> <hi rend="bold">as</hi> <hi rend="bold">we said above:</hi> he who killed [shall pay] <hi rend="italic">ƿer</hi> [wergeld] and <hi rend="italic">ƿite</hi> [fine], <hi rend="spaced">but each of his companions</hi> CXX shillings.
crib.Af_31-1|III 5–8: If that association <hi rend="spaced">which we have called</hi> <hi rend="italic">hloth</hi> [band] has committed <hi rend="spaced">these homicides</hi> and afterwards wishes to deny this by oath, <hi rend="spaced">then all those accused together</hi> shall pay the price of the slain man, <hi rend="spaced">and all together</hi> one forfeiture, as befits the price, <hi rend="bold">which the English call <hi rend="italic">be ƿeres mæðe</hi> [according to the measure of the wer]</hi> . . . .
crib.Af_44|III 9–39: <hi rend="spaced">The compensation for a wounded head is</hi>: if the bones are <hi rend="bold">without</hi> <hi rend="spaced">perforation</hi>, XXX shillings.
crib.Af_44-1|III 9–39: <hi rend="spaced">And if the outer</hi> <hi rend="spaced">bone is perforated</hi>, XV shillings.
crib.Af_45|III 9–39: If within the hair there is a wound <hi rend="spaced">of one inch</hi> long, he shall give <seg type="recension">(compensate)</seg> one shilling.
crib.Af_45-1|III 9–39: If it is outside the hair <hi rend="spaced">and of the same size, two</hi> shillings <hi rend="spaced">shall be</hi> the compensation.
crib.Af_46|III 9–39: If someone's ear <hi rend="spaced">is cut off</hi>, he shall compensate XXX shillings.
crib.Af_46-1|III 9–39: If the hearing <hi rend="spaced">is stopped up, so that he cannot hear</hi>, he shall compensate LX shillings.
crib.Af_47|III 9–39: If someone's eye is cut out, <hi rend="spaced">the compensation will be such</hi>: sixty-six shillings and six pence and a third part of a penny.
crib.Af_47-1|III 9–39: And if the eye <hi rend="spaced">remains within the head</hi> and yet he can see nothing with that eye, a third part <hi rend="bold">shall stand</hi> <hi rend="bold">in</hi> <hi rend="spaced">the compensation</hi>.
crib.Af_48|III 9–39: If someone's <hi rend="bold">jaw</hi> is cut off, he shall compensate LX shillings.
crib.Af_49|III 9–39: If someone's front tooth <seg type="recension">(that is, incisor)</seg> is pulled out, he shall compensate eight shillings.
crib.Af_49-1|III 9–39: If <hi rend="spaced">however</hi> a tooth <seg type="recension">(<hi rend="bold">canine</hi>)</seg>, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">wengthoþ</hi> [cheek-tooth], is knocked out, he shall compensate four shillings.
crib.Af_49-2|III 9–39: <hi rend="bold">The jaw-tooth,</hi> that is <hi rend="italic">tuxl</hi> [tusk] <seg type="recension">(or <hi rend="bold">molars</hi>)</seg> of a man, <hi rend="spaced">is paid for with fifteen shillings.</hi>
crib.Af_50|III 9–39: If someone's jaw-bone <hi rend="spaced">is broken</hi>, he shall compensate fifteen shillings.
crib.Af_50-1|III 9–39: The chin <seg type="recension">(that is <hi rend="italic">cinban</hi> [chin-bone])</seg>, if it is split, he shall compensate twelve shillings.
crib.Af_51|III 9–39: If someone's gullet, that is <hi rend="italic">þrotbolle</hi> [throat-boll], <hi rend="spaced">is pierced</hi>, he shall compensate twelve shillings.
crib.Af_52|III 9–39: If someone's tongue <hi rend="spaced">is cut out</hi>, its compensation [is] as [that] of an eye.
crib.Af_53|III 9–39: If anyone is wounded in the shoulders so that the fluid <seg type="recension">(that is <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">mæri</hi></hi>)</seg> comes out, he shall compensate thirty shillings.
crib.Af_54|III 9–39: If anyone breaks someone's upper arm, he shall compensate fifteen shillings.
crib.Af_55|III 9–39: If anyone breaks <hi rend="spaced">both</hi> <hi rend="spaced">arms</hi> of someone, he shall compensate thirty shillings.
crib.Af_56|III 9–39: And <hi rend="spaced">he who</hi> <hi rend="spaced">cuts off</hi> a thumb shall compensate thirty shillings.
crib.Af_56-1|III 9–39: If <hi rend="spaced">anyone</hi> <hi rend="spaced">cuts off</hi> the nail of the thumb, he shall compensate five shillings.
crib.Af_57|III 9–39: The second finger <hi rend="spaced">is called</hi> index <hi rend="spaced">or</hi> pointer; <hi rend="spaced">its price is</hi> fifteen shillings; its nail <hi rend="bold">V</hi> shillings.
crib.Af_58|III 9–39: The third finger, <hi rend="spaced">which is called the unchaste: its price is</hi> twelve shillings, and its nail two shillings.
