crib.Af_59|III 9–39: <hi rend="spaced">The fourth, the ring finger; the price</hi> <hi rend="spaced">of it</hi> XVII shillings, and its nail four shillings.
crib.Af_60|III 9–39: The fifth, the ear finger; its price nine shillings, and its nail one shilling <hi rend="bold"><seg type="recension">(XII pence)</seg></hi>.
crib.Af_61|III 9–39: If anyone is wounded in the groin <seg type="recension">(that is <hi rend="italic">grin</hi>)</seg>, it shall be compensated with thirty shillings.
crib.Af_61-1|III 9–39: But if it has been pierced right through, <hi rend="spaced">for each hole</hi> XX shillings, <hi rend="spaced">that is, for one hole</hi> XX <hi rend="spaced">shillings and for the other likewise</hi>.
crib.Af_62|III 9–39: If a man's thigh is pierced, he shall compensate thirty shillings;
crib.Af_62-1|III 9–39: and if it is broken, likewise.
crib.Af_63|III 9–39: If the shin is pierced below the knee, he shall compensate twelve shillings.
crib.Af_63-1|III 9–39: But if it is <hi rend="bold">above</hi> the knee, thirty shillings.
crib.Af_64|III 9–39: The first toe <hi rend="spaced">is valued at</hi> twenty shillings,
crib.Af_65|III 9–39: If anyone is so wounded in the genitals that he cannot beget a child, he shall compensate <hi rend="spaced">his price</hi> with eighty shillings.
crib.Af_66|III 9–39: If someone's arm <hi rend="spaced">is cut off</hi> with the hand, before the elbow, he shall compensate LXXX shillings.
crib.Af_66-1|III 9–39: Every wound <hi rend="spaced">made</hi> outside the hair and before the sleeves <hi rend="bold">and before the elbow</hi> and <hi rend="spaced">before the knee shall have a double price</hi>.
crib.Af_67|III 9–39: If the <hi rend="spaced">roast of the kidneys, which</hi> <hi rend="spaced">the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">lendebræde</hi> [loin-roast], is entirely cut through, he shall compensate sixty shillings.
crib.Af_67-1|III 9–39: But if it is stabbed into, he shall compensate fifteen shillings.
crib.Af_67-2|III 9–39: If it is pierced through, he shall compensate XXX shillings.
crib.Af_68|III 9–39: If anyone is wounded in the shoulder, <hi rend="spaced">if he can live, let compensation be made</hi> to him with eighty shillings.
crib.Af_69|III 9–39: If anyone strikes the hand <hi rend="spaced">of another from outside, if it can be healed, let there be given to him</hi> twenty shillings.
crib.Af_69-1|III 9–39: If <hi rend="spaced">however</hi> half <hi rend="spaced">is cut off</hi>, XL shillings <hi rend="spaced">shall be paid in compensation</hi> to him.
crib.Af_70|III 9–39: If anyone breaks a rib <hi rend="spaced">of a man</hi> with the skin intact, he shall compensate him ten shillings.
crib.Af_70-1|III 9–39: But if the skin is broken, and bone <hi rend="spaced">is extracted</hi> from it, fifteen shillings.
crib.Af_71|III 9–39: If someone's eye, foot or hand <hi rend="spaced">is cut off</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">these three</hi> <hi rend="spaced">have</hi> an equal price, <hi rend="spaced">namely</hi> sixty-six shillings and six pence and a third part of a penny.
crib.Af_72|III 9–39: If someone's leg is cut off <hi rend="spaced">up to</hi> the knee, eighty shillings <hi rend="spaced">shall be paid in compensation</hi> to him.
crib.Af_73|III 9–39: If anyone <hi rend="spaced">cuts off</hi> the shoulders <hi rend="spaced">of another</hi>, he shall compensate twenty shillings.
crib.Af_74|III 9–39: If <hi rend="spaced">however he has been so struck</hi> that bone is drawn out from it, he shall compensate him XV shillings.
crib.Af_75|III 9–39: If the great sinew <hi rend="spaced">is cut</hi> <hi rend="spaced">and it can</hi> <hi rend="spaced">be healed</hi>, twelve shillings <hi rend="spaced">shall be paid in compensation</hi>.
crib.Af_75-1|III 9–39: But if he is lame <hi rend="spaced">because of the cutting of the sinew</hi>, so that he cannot be cured, he shall compensate thirty shillings.
crib.Af_76|III 9–39: If the more delicate <seg type="recension">(that is, smaller)</seg> sinews <hi rend="spaced">are cut</hi>, he shall compensate VI shillings.
crib.Af_77|III 9–39: If someone's <hi rend="spaced">sinews and veins</hi> on the neck are so <hi rend="spaced">cut that he cannot raise his neck, and yet he lives thus disfigured</hi>, a hundred shillings shall be given him as compensation, unless the wise <hi rend="spaced">adjudge</hi> him a greater <hi rend="spaced">right</hi>. . . .
crib.InCn_III-40|III 40: <hi rend="small">If anyone has lent his weapons to another, and he <hi rend="spaced">to whom they were lent</hi> kills a man with them, he himself who lent the weapons shall pay a third part of the price and of the forfeiture; or he shall clear himself, that it was not <hi rend="spaced">his counsel nor his will</hi>.</hi>
crib.Af_23|III 41: . . . If a dog tears or kills a man, the first time he <hi rend="spaced">whose dog it is</hi> shall compensate him six shillings; and if <hi rend="spaced">after this</hi> he feeds the same dog, he shall pay twelve shillings; the third <hi rend="spaced">time, however, if it</hi> <hi rend="spaced">does the same, its master</hi> shall <hi rend="spaced">compensate</hi> thirty shillings.
crib.Af_23-1|III 41: And <hi rend="spaced">although</hi> the dog perishes in such a deed, nevertheless the compensation <hi rend="spaced">shall be paid</hi>.
crib.Af_23-2|III 41: <hi rend="spaced">But if the dog has done still more</hi> <hi rend="spaced">harms than these</hi>, and <hi rend="spaced">the aforesaid master</hi> <seg type="recension">(its)</seg> still keeps it, he shall compensate the full <hi rend="spaced">price of the one to whom harm</hi> it has done, <hi rend="spaced">whether it be the violation of</hi> a scar <hi rend="spaced">or whether it be</hi> <hi rend="spaced">something else</hi> . . . .
crib.Mirce_1|III 42–43.4: The price <hi rend="spaced">of a man</hi> <hi rend="bold">whom we have named above</hi> <hi rend="bold"><hi rend="italic">ceorlman</hi></hi>, according to the law of the Mercians, is CC shillings.
crib.Mirce_1-1|III 42–43.4: [43] The price of a free man of rank (thegn), <hi rend="spaced">that is</hi> of a <hi rend="italic">þegenes</hi> [thegn's], is <hi rend="spaced">six times</hi> as much, that is twelve times C shillings.
crib.Mirce_2|III 42–43.4: [43, 1] But six times as much will be the single price of the king, that is <hi rend="bold">two hundred</hi> XX pounds.
crib.Mirce_3|III 42–43.4: [43, 2] So much according to justice is the price <hi rend="spaced">of the king</hi>.
crib.Mirce_3-1|III 42–43.4: [43, 3] But because of the <hi rend="spaced">excellence</hi> of the royal dignity it is fitting <hi rend="spaced">to give</hi> again just as much.
crib.Mirce_4|III 42–43.4: [43, 4] The kinsmen <seg type="recension">(however)</seg> <hi rend="spaced">of the king</hi> justly <hi rend="spaced">ought to have the single</hi> price of him <seg type="recension">(the king)</seg>, and the people the <hi rend="spaced">other</hi>.
crib.InCn_III-44|III 44: <hi rend="small">The oath of a noble, <hi rend="spaced">whom</hi><hi rend="spaced"> indeed</hi><hi rend="spaced"> the English</hi><hi rend="spaced"> call</hi> <hi rend="italic">tƿelfhende</hi></hi> <seg type="recension"><hi rend="small">(man)</hi></seg><hi rend="small">, <hi rend="spaced">ought to stand and</hi> be worth the oath of six villeins, because his price, that is <hi rend="italic">ƿeregeld</hi> [wergeld], is [that] of six villeins.</hi>
crib.InCn_III-45|III 45: <hi rend="small">The oath of a priest</hi> regularly [by a rule] <hi rend="small">living is worth just as much </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="small">(namely)</hi></seg><hi rend="small"> as [that] of a noble, on account of the seven ecclesiastical orders.</hi>
crib.Had_1|III 45.1–45.3: <hi rend="spaced">For</hi> there are seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; and seven times daily <hi rend="spaced">priests and other servants of God in</hi> <hi rend="spaced">churches</hi> ought to praise God and continually intercede for the Christian people.
crib.Had_1-2|III 45.1–45.3: And therefore whoever <hi rend="spaced">desires or has done</hi> harm to such, <hi rend="spaced">it is necessary</hi> that he make amends for it with sevenfold compensation.
crib.Had_2|III 45.1–45.3: [45, 2] [2—8] And if <hi rend="spaced">anyone kills a priest, besides his</hi> just price, he shall compensate <hi rend="spaced">for each order</hi> twenty shillings, <hi rend="spaced">namely for the order of doorkeeper</hi> twenty shillings, likewise <hi rend="spaced">for the exorcist</hi> <hi rend="spaced">again</hi> twenty shillings, and so <hi rend="spaced">through the orders</hi>, until <hi rend="spaced">it passes the priesthood</hi>. [45, 3] <hi rend="spaced">These seven pounds for the seven orders will be outside the price which is called</hi> <hi rend="italic">þeregeld</hi>.
crib.Had_9-1|III 45.1–45.3: [9, 1] And <seg type="recension">(these)</seg> shall justly be the bishop's <hi rend="bold">and the poor's.</hi>
crib.InCn_III-45-4|III 45.4: These are the customs of the kings among the English:
crib.InCn_III-46|III 46: All the rights of the cities <seg type="recension">(are the king's)</seg>; and his food-rent [with all the things that pertain to that food-rent; the charter of allod (bookland) for eternal inheritance; the forfeiture of allod; and the price of those who hold allod, when they forfeit themselves so deeply; the forfeiture for war, which the English call <hi rend="italic">ferdƿíte</hi> [fyrd-wite], in the land of all his men;
crib.InCn_III-47|III 47: the feeding of a proclaimed exile, which the English say <seg type="recension">(call)</seg> <hi rend="italic">bebodenes utlage</hi> [a commanded outlaw];
crib.InCn_III-48|III 48: also the feeding of robbers hiding in the woods who plunder and kill others <seg type="recension">(men)</seg> — whom the English call <hi rend="italic">fléman</hi> [fugitives] —; every robber proclaimed outside [the law]; the life or the price of a public robber.
crib.InCn_III-49|III 49: Invasion of a house or court, which is called <hi rend="italic">rihthamsócne</hi> [true hamsocn], if he who has done it has been proclaimed outside his bounds, then, if he comes to make amends, the king shall have it.
crib.InCn_III-50|III 50: Also breach of the peace, which is called <hi rend="italic">grithbrece</hi> [grith-breach]: if peace is commanded on the king's part in the shire (court) or in the hundred, whoever breaks it after that shall make amends to the king.
crib.InCn_III-50-1|III 50.1: The amends for a broken bridge on the king's road.
crib.InCn_III-51|III 51: In the land of all men, according to ancient custom, the amends for broken peace of the church shall be in common the king's and the bishop's.
crib.InCn_III-51-1|III 51.1: And the king has many other customs which befit him.
crib.InCn_III-52|III 52: Whoever has a boundary next to the king's land, let him fence against the king or keep watch, or acquire it by goodwill or by price, if he wishes to have any <seg type="recension">(advantage)</seg> easement in that land.
crib.InCn_III-53|III 53: It was an ancient custom that every ecclesiastical and secular amends was common to the king and the bishop.
crib.InCn_III-54|III 54: This too each man ought to know, that, if for any forfeiture which pertains to God money is taken by the bishop or by any other, the bishop ought to distribute that same money to churches and to the poor.
crib.InCn_III-55|III 55: The earl's rights according to the English, these are common with the king: the third penny in towns where a market has come together and in the punishment of thieves; and the comital towns which pertain to his shire; and to have all the customs of free men of rank (thegns) doubly, namely double <hi rend="italic">mund</hi> [protection], double <hi rend="italic">manbote</hi> [man-amends] and <seg type="recension">(double)</seg> forfeiture; he must also have a double price, that is <hi rend="italic">þere</hi> [wer].
crib.InCn_III-56|III 56: <hi rend="small">In the law of Kent Christ Church and the king and the archbishop have a like and equally dear contempt-fine, </hi><hi rend="spaced"><hi rend="small">which the English call</hi></hi><hi rend="small"> <hi rend="italic">mundbrece</hi> [breach of protection].</hi>
crib.InCn_III-56-1|III 56.1: <hi rend="small">And in that law the archbishop's property <hi rend="spaced">shall be repaid</hi> elevenfold, but the king's property shall <hi rend="spaced">not</hi> be repaid <hi rend="spaced">except</hi> ninefold.</hi>
crib.InCn_III-56-2|III 56.2: <hi rend="small">Other[wise] the archbishop and the <hi rend="spaced">king's son</hi> <hi rend="spaced">by a lawful wife have a like secular right</hi></hi> in many things, <hi rend="small">that is in the contempt-fine,</hi> in the amends for a slain man, which is called <hi rend="italic">manbote</hi> [man-amends], and in many other different things, that is in paying the <hi rend="italic">þere</hi> [wer] price and the forfeiture<seg type="recension">(m)</seg>, both equally great and dear.
crib.InCn_III-57|III 57: The bishop and the earl have many equal secular laws; indeed formerly they had all the same, on account of the excellence of their order.
crib.InCn_III-58|III 58: Bishops above all <seg type="recension">(should have)</seg> ecclesiastical correction and Christian lordship over all, whom they <hi rend="small">ought to teach and to lead before the judgment of God and</hi> to go before.
crib.InCn_III-58-1|III 58.1: In many places, however, according to justice, in their own land and in their towns they ought to have the setting of the hundred, which the English call <hi rend="italic">hundrædsétene</hi> [hundred-session]; and the price of thieves <seg type="recension">(proclaimed)</seg> within their bounds; and unaccomplished invasion, which the English call <seg type="recension">(which is called)</seg> <hi rend="italic">unƿorhtre hamsocne</hi> [attempted hamsocn]; and <hi rend="italic">toll ⁊ team</hi>; and the correction of thieves, until he is condemned to death;
crib.InCn_III-59|III 59: so also moneyers and <hi rend="italic">púndæres</hi> or weighers; and places of the ordeals of iron or water; their own measures and weights; and many various customs, which those established who loved God's honour <seg type="recension">(and justice)</seg>.
crib.Gethyn_1|III 60–63.1: [60] It was an <hi rend="spaced">ancient</hi> <hi rend="bold">law of the English</hi> that <hi rend="spaced">their</hi> <hi rend="spaced">people</hi> and customs were held in honour; and <hi rend="bold">by counsel</hi> [rights] were given to <seg type="recension">(every)</seg> each according to the measure of each, <hi rend="spaced">to earl and villein</hi>, to the free man of rank (thegn) and to the <hi rend="bold">lesser free man</hi>.
crib.Gethyn_2|III 60–63.1: [60, 1] And if a villein had so prospered <hi rend="bold">by his own worth</hi> that he fully had five hides of his own <hi rend="spaced">allod</hi> <hi rend="bold">and his own church</hi> and bell-house <hi rend="bold">and kitchen</hi> and gate, a seat and special office in the king's hall, then thenceforth he was worthy of the honour of nobility, <hi rend="spaced">which the English call</hi> <hi rend="italic">þegen<hi rend="bold">scipes</hi> þurðe</hi> [worthy of thegnship].
crib.Gethyn_3|III 60–63.1: [61] <hi rend="bold">If</hi> moreover a free man of rank, that is a <hi rend="italic">þegen</hi> [thegn], <hi rend="spaced">had so advanced</hi> that he served the king and rode <hi rend="spaced">in his stead</hi> on the king's <hi rend="bold">mission</hi>, such a one, if he had <hi rend="spaced">another under him</hi> who held five hides for the king's <hi rend="bold">expedition</hi> and had served his lord in the king's hall and had three times gone to the king as his lord's messenger, such a one, <hi rend="spaced">I say</hi>, <hi rend="spaced">can</hi> thenceforth swear the fore-oath for his lord, <hi rend="bold">which we named above</hi> <hi rend="italic">foraþ</hi> [fore-oath], <hi rend="bold">in various matters,</hi> wherever there is need.
crib.Gethyn_4|III 60–63.1: [61, 1] But whoever did not have such a one would <hi rend="spaced">do</hi> it by himself <hi rend="spaced">or</hi> go without.
crib.Gethyn_5|III 60–63.1: [61, 2] And if a free man of rank had so risen that he became an earl, he had <hi rend="spaced">all his rights as</hi> an earl.
crib.Gethyn_6|III 60–63.1: [62] If a merchant had three times crossed the sea at his own expense, such a one was thenceforth worthy of nobility, <hi rend="spaced">which they call</hi> <hi rend="italic">þegenrihtes þurðe</hi> [worthy of thegn-right].
crib.Gethyn_7|III 60–63.1: [63] So <hi rend="spaced">also</hi> a cleric too, who by learning had advanced so far that he had orders and served Christ <hi rend="bold">in chastity</hi>, he was then judged <hi rend="spaced">by right in all things</hi> to be bound to have <hi rend="bold">nobility</hi>.
crib.Gethyn_8|III 60–63.1: [63, 1] And if it <hi rend="bold">should happen</hi> that someone has injured an ordained man or a stranger, then the king and the bishop ought <hi rend="spaced">justly</hi> to make amends for it as quickly as they could.
crib.InCn_III-64|III 64: <hi rend="small">The horn of an ox <hi rend="spaced">is paid for</hi> with ten pence and of a cow with two pence;</hi>
crib.InCn_III-64-1|III 64.1: <hi rend="small">the tail </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="small">(however)</hi></seg><hi rend="small"> of an ox </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="small">(is paid for)</hi></seg><hi rend="small"> with one shilling and of a cow </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="small">(is paid for)</hi></seg><hi rend="small"> with five pence; the eye of an ox </hi><seg type="recension"><hi rend="small">(is paid for)</hi></seg><hi rend="small"> with five pence and of a cow</hi> four <seg type="recension">(pence)</seg>.
